lead: At a few gigahertz, high power still comes from electrons flying through vacuum, not from a transistor. A microwave tube takes a DC beam from an electron gun and makes it hand energy to an RF field. Klystrons amplify, reflex klystrons oscillate, magnetrons deliver pulsed megawatts, and travelling wave tubes give wideband gain. You find them in radar transmitters, satellite ground stations, microwave ovens and older laboratory benches. This chapter shows the mechanism of each tube, the mode it runs in, and how gain, bandwidth and efficiency differ between them.
prereq: You need: waveguide modes and cavity resonators from Unit 1, and the port picture of a microwave component from 4.1 S-parameters.

sections.h3: Two-cavity klystron: velocity modulation and bunching

blocks.text: A two-cavity klystron is an amplifier. An electron gun makes a beam with DC voltage V₀ and current I₀. The beam crosses the gap of the input cavity, where a small RF voltage adds energy to some electrons and removes it from others. Electrons that cross the gap while the RF field accelerates them leave just after the reference electron and travel faster, so they catch up with the slower electrons that crossed just before them. A quarter cycle later the beam is a train of dense bunches, one per RF cycle. The output cavity converts part of their kinetic energy into output power. A collector absorbs the spent beam.
v(t) = v₀ [1 + (V₁ / 2V₀) sin ωt],   v₀ = √(2eV₀ / m)
blocks.where: V₀ is the beam voltage in volts, v₀ the entry speed in m/s, V₁ the RF gap voltage, ω = 2πf the angular frequency, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
X is the bunching parameter (dimensionless), θ the drift transit angle in radians and L the drift length in metres. Bunching is strongest near X = 1.84.

items: Gain of a multicavity klystron is about 30 dB to 60 dB.
Bandwidth is narrow, roughly 1 % to 5 % of the centre frequency, set by the cavity Q.
Efficiency is 15 % to 40 % for two cavities and up to about 60 % with more cavities and a depressed collector.
Power runs from watts to megawatts CW at UHF and microwave bands.

sections.h3: Reflex klystron: one cavity, repeller, transit-time modes

blocks.text: A reflex klystron is an oscillator built from one cavity. A repeller electrode behind the cavity is held negative, so it slows the electrons, stops them and sends them back through the same gap. Electrons that return while the gap field opposes them give energy to the cavity. That is feedback without a second cavity.

blocks.where: t is the round-trip transit time in the repeller space in seconds, f the oscillation frequency in hertz and n the mode number. Each n is a separate mode with its own power and frequency.

blocks.text: Changing the repeller voltage changes the electron speed and so the transit time t. That shifts the frequency, which is electronic tuning. A tuning screw changes the cavity size, which is mechanical tuning. Output is a few milliwatts to a few watts, efficiency is 1 % to 20 %, and the tube served as a local oscillator in radar receivers and as a bench source.

sections.h3: Magnetron: crossed fields and the π-mode

blocks.text: A magnetron has a central cylindrical cathode and an anode block hollowed into N resonant cavities. A DC voltage puts a radial electric field between cathode and anode. A permanent magnet puts a steady axial magnetic field along the same axis. The two fields are crossed, so electrons do not travel straight; they curve, and near the correct field they form a rotating spoke that passes energy into the cavities.

blocks.where: f_c is the cyclotron frequency in gigahertz, B the magnetic flux density in tesla, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

blocks.text: In the π-mode, neighbouring cavities oscillate 180° out of phase. This mode gives the best efficiency and is fixed by strapping the cavities together. The oscillation frequency comes from the cavity dimensions, near 3 GHz for S-band radar and 2.45 GHz for a microwave oven. Pulsed output reaches megawatts, efficiency is 40 % to 70 %, and bandwidth is narrow because the cavities resonate.

sections.h3: Travelling wave tube: helix and broadband gain

blocks.text: A travelling wave tube (TWT) has no resonant cavity in the interaction region. A helix wound inside the vacuum tube slows the RF wave so that its axial speed matches the electron beam. The beam speed is set slightly above the wave speed, so electrons give energy to the wave continuously along the whole length instead of at one gap.

blocks.where: v_p is the axial phase velocity of the wave on the helix in m/s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, p the helix pitch (turn spacing) in metres and a the helix radius in metres.

blocks.text: Because the helix is not resonant, one tube covers more than an octave. Gain is 20 dB to 40 dB, efficiency 10 % to 20 %, and CW output goes from a few watts to kilowatts. The price of bandwidth is low efficiency and a long, delicate structure.

examples.question: A two-cavity klystron has a beam voltage of 2 kV, a beam current of 50 mA and an RF output power of 40 W. Find the DC input power and the efficiency.
steps: Convert to base units: V₀ = 2 kV = 2000 V, I₀ = 50 mA = 0.050 A, P_rf = 40 W.
DC input power P_dc = V₀ × I₀ = 2000 V × 0.050 A = 100 W.
Check the units: watts divided by watts is dimensionless, so the answer is a plain percentage.
examples.answer: The DC input power is 100 W and the efficiency is 40 %.
examples.check:
V0 = 2000.0
I0 = 0.050
P_rf = 40.0
P_dc = V0 * I0
eta = P_rf / P_dc * 100.0
print(P_dc)
print(eta)

traps: A klystron and a reflex klystron are different devices: the first is a two-cavity or multicavity amplifier, the second a single-cavity oscillator. A question about the drift tube is not about the reflex tube.
π-mode means neighbouring cavities differ by 180° in phase, not that the tube runs at π radians per second. Other modes exist and give lower efficiency at the wrong frequency.
Efficiency uses the DC input V₀I₀. kV × mA already gives watts, so converting both or neither is safe. Converting only one (kV with A, or V with mA) gives an answer that is wrong by 10³.
The collector heat is loss, not output power. Never add it to P_rf when computing efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the job of the drift tube in a two-cavity klystron?
quiz.a: It gives the faster electrons time to catch the slower ones, so the velocity modulation from the input cavity becomes current bunches at the output cavity.

quiz.q: State the transit-time condition for a reflex klystron to oscillate in mode n.
quiz.a: The round trip in the repeller space must take (n + 3/4) RF periods, that is t = (n + 3/4)/f, with n = 0, 1, 2, …

quiz.q: Why does a reflex klystron oscillate while a two-cavity klystron only amplifies?
quiz.a: In the reflex tube the same beam is turned back through the same cavity, so the cavity supplies its own feedback and needs no input. The two-cavity tube has separate input and output cavities, so it needs an external drive and only amplifies.

quiz.q: Why is a TWT broadband while a klystron is narrowband?
quiz.a: A klystron depends on resonant cavities, and a cavity works over a narrow band around its resonant frequency. A TWT uses a non-resonant helix in which the wave speed matches the beam over a wide range, so the interaction survives over an octave or more.

quiz.q: A klystron runs at beam voltage 3 kV and beam current 40 mA, and gives 30 W of RF output. Find P_dc and η.
A reflex klystron is switched on but gives no output. Slightly changing the repeller voltage restores the output. Explain.
quiz.a: The tube oscillates only when the round-trip transit time equals (n + 3/4)/f. If the repeller voltage is wrong, electrons return at the wrong phase, take energy from the cavity instead of giving it, and oscillation stops. Changing the repeller voltage changes the return time and brings the tube back into a mode. Each mode sits at a different repeller voltage.

quiz.q: Compare a magnetron and a TWT as the transmitter tube of a pulsed radar.
quiz.a: A magnetron is an oscillator giving megawatt pulses at 40 % to 70 % efficiency, but it is narrowband and a free-running magnetron has no fixed phase from pulse to pulse, which blocks pulse-Doppler processing. A TWT is a broadband amplifier at 10 % to 20 % efficiency with lower peak power, but it is coherent and can amplify a coded waveform, so it is used where wide bandwidth or phase coherence matters.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same beam–wave interaction is pushed to millimetre waves in gyrotrons, which use a strong magnetic field and fast cyclotron motion rather than a slow-wave structure. Coupled-cavity and folded-waveguide TWTs trade bandwidth for more power at high frequency. Space TWTs are the reason satellite downlinks are still quoted with tube output power in watts. Inductive output tubes (IOTs) replaced klystrons in many digital television transmitters. Search for helix TWT, folded waveguide, gyrotron and IOT if you want to read further.
